questions.stem: A logging library was compiled with javac 11 (--release 11) and is never rebuilt. Its toString() methods build text with +. The service using it moves from JDK 11 to JDK 21. On JDK 21, which code joins the parts of those strings?

options.text: Code that JDK 21 generates when each call site first runs, since the class file names a bootstrap method and a recipe
options.says: the + compiled to invokedynamic with StringConcatFactory as bootstrap; the running JDK builds the code at first execution

options.text: Code that javac 11 chose when it compiled the library, since the class file records the concatenation strategy
options.says: javac records only the recipe and the bootstrap method; the strategy belongs to the JDK that links the call site

options.text: A StringBuilder chain that javac 11 emitted, since only class files compiled for release 21 use invokedynamic
options.says: javac has emitted invokedynamic for + since release 9; only release 8 or -XDstringConcat=inline gives a StringBuilder chain

options.text: A StringBuilder chain that JDK 21 substitutes, since the JVM rewrites the + of class files older than its own release
options.says: the JVM does not rewrite old class files; it links their invokedynamic through the JDK 21 bootstrap

origin.section: invokedynamic Leaves the Choice of Code to the First Run

questions.stem: Right after a deploy, the first call to formatOrderLine(order), a method that returns "#" + id + " x" + qty, takes 7 ms; every later call takes a few microseconds. The Order class was loaded and used by other code well before that call. What explains the slow first call?

options.text: The first execution ran the bootstrap method behind the method's invokedynamic, which built the code that later calls reuse
options.says: the first execution of an invokedynamic calls its bootstrap method, which generates the code and links the call site; later executions go to the linked code

options.text: The first execution ran the JIT compiler on the whole method, which built the machine code that later calls reuse
options.says: a method starts interpreted and is compiled only once it is hot (unit 10.5.3); the first-call cost here is the bootstrap

options.text: The first execution allocated a StringBuilder for the method's concatenation, whose buffer later calls reuse
options.says: the method contains no StringBuilder: it is one invokedynamic, and no buffer survives between calls

options.text: The first execution loaded the Order class for the method's parameters, whose metadata later calls reuse
options.says: the stem says Order was loaded before; the cost is the invokedynamic bootstrap

origin.section: invokedynamic Leaves the Choice of Code to the First Run

questions.stem: A switch on a String has the labels case "Ab", case "BC" and a default; both labels have hashCode() 2113. It is called with a String "BC" read from a file. Which branch runs?

options.text: The "BC" branch, since javac follows the hash match with an equals check against each label sharing that hash
options.says: javac emits a lookupswitch on hashCode(), then an equals for each label with that hash, then a tableswitch on the matching index

options.text: The "BC" branch, since javac gives each of the two colliding labels a key of its own in the lookupswitch
options.says: the lookupswitch keys are hash values, so the two labels share one key and are told apart by equals

options.text: The "Ab" branch, since the hash match leads straight to the first label declared with that hash
options.says: the hash only leads to the labels that share it; equals decides between them

options.text: The "Ab" branch, since javac keeps one label per hash in the lookupswitch and folds the later one into it
options.says: javac keeps every label; colliding labels go into the same bucket and each is compared with equals

origin.section: A switch on Strings Is a hashCode lookupswitch Followed by equals

questions.stem: A method reads try { return loadConfig(); } finally { return cached; } and is compiled with @SuppressWarnings("finally"). loadConfig() throws IllegalStateException. What does the caller see, and why?

options.text: It gets cached and no exception, since the exception path's copy of the finally code ends in a return, not an athrow
options.says: the any handler saves the exception in a local, runs its copy of the finally code, and that copy returns, so nothing rethrows it

options.text: It gets cached and no exception, since javac leaves the try out of the exception table when the finally returns
options.says: the exception table still sends the try's range to an any handler; the handler is what ends in a return

options.text: It gets the IllegalStateException, since the JVM rethrows any pending exception once a finally block completes
options.says: there is no finally instruction and no pending exception in the JVM; the rethrow is an athrow javac copies, and here it was replaced by a return

options.text: It gets the IllegalStateException, since a return in finally only replaces the value of a try that returned normally
options.says: javac copies the return onto the exception path too, so it replaces the rethrow as well

origin.section: finally Is Copied Onto Every Exit, and a return There Replaces the athrow
